fixes.explanation: That's it. Paul writes, "And my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:19). The measure is God's riches, not our pockets. That's a cookie jar with no bottom, friend.
Paul doesn't say silent. He says he has learned to be content regardless of his circumstances (Philippians 4:11). Content means settled, not hushed. Settled is the word to hold onto.

That's the one. Paul says, "I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength." (Philippians 4:13). The strength comes from Christ, and Paul says so plainly. It's right there in the verse, no gym wall needed.
A fun word, but not Paul's. He says they have done well to share in his affliction (Philippians 4:14). Affliction is the hard part, and they joined him there.

Most of them would be quite a crowd, friend. But Paul says, "…no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving." (Philippians 4:15). Besides the Philippians, no church did. That makes their giving stand out even more.

True. Paul says, "I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts from Epaphroditus." (Philippians 4:18). The gifts came to him through Epaphroditus. Paul's cup was full and then some.

It's actually true. Paul says, "I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts from Epaphroditus." (Philippians 4:18). The gifts came to him through Epaphroditus. Paul isn't just getting by, friend. He says he has more than he needs.

That's the phrase. Paul says the gifts are "…a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God." (Philippians 4:18). Gifts given to Paul became something pleasing to God. Your kindness is never small to Him.
A tithe of the harvest isn't Paul's word here. He calls the gifts "…a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God." (Philippians 4:18). Fragrant offering is the one.

Paul names a different measure. He says God will supply all their needs "…according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:19). The measure in that verse is God's riches. How much they gave isn't the measure he names.

Yes, Caesar's household. Paul says, "All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar." (Philippians 4:22). Caesar was the Roman emperor. Saints from his household are sending hello to Philippi, friend.
